# Saṅkiccajātaka (Ja 530)

**ID:** Ja 530  
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Saṅkiccajātaka  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul2.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul2.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Saṅkiccajātaka* (Ja 530) is a narrative text preserved in the Pali Jātaka collection. According to the traditional background narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha related the tale while staying at Jīvaka's mango grove in connection with King Ajātasattu's murder of his father King Bimbisāra [Wu 2012]. The frame story adapts elements of the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* narrative cycle, illustrating how Ajātasattu—haunted by guilt and terrified of descent into hell after following the counsel of Devadatta—sought out the Buddha as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and found peace of mind [Wu 2012]. The story of the past reveals that the king had likewise murdered his father in a former birth [Tan 2002].

Literarily, Maurice Winternitz characterizes the core story as an *itihāsa* dialogue resembling passages from the ancient Purāṇas [Winternitz 1933]. In the verse narrative, King Brahmadatta receives his former domestic chaplain, the sage Saṅkicca, and inquires about the fate of sinners in the hereafter; in response, Saṅkicca delivers a lengthy discourse containing vivid descriptions of hells and the retribution awaiting wrongdoers [Winternitz 1933].

 Shared verses or citations appear in the *Petavatthu* (Pv 10, Pv 19, Pv 38), the *Niddesa* (Mnd 15, Cnd 23), and the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 20.3).

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Passage-level parallels: AN 3.36 Devadūtasutta; MN 129 (PTS MN iii 163) Bālapaṇḍita Sutta; MN 130 (PTS MN iii 178) Devadūta Sutta
- Resembling parallels: Thig 12.1 Puṇṇātherīgāthā
- Mentioned in: Pv 10 Khallāṭiyapetivatthu; Mnd 15 Attadaṇḍasuttaniddesa; Cnd 23 Khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa; Kv 20.3 Nirayapālakathā; Pv 19 Dhanapālaseṭṭhipetavatthu; Pv 38 Nandakapetavatthu

**Sources**

- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, A History of Indian Literature, Vol. II (1933) — Described the itihāsa dialogue structure, the purāṇic tone, and Saṅkicca's sermon on hell.
- [Wu 2012] Juan Wu, From Perdition to Awakening: Study of Legends of the Salvation of the Patricide Ajatasatru in Indian Buddhism (2012) — Analyzed the frame story, its relation to the Sāmaññaphala-sutta cycle, and Ajātasattu's repentance.
- [Tan 2002] Piya Tan, Buddha & His Disciples: Profiles and Perspectives in Self-Discovery (2002, 2004) — Noted the past-life patricide motif associated with Ajātasattu.
